text: India is one of the best places in the world to find [[fossil|fossils]], because its rocks record a long and unusual journey. Over the last 150 million years or so, [[@india-drift|India drifted]] north across an ocean as an island, then crashed into Asia and pushed up the Himalaya. Each chapter left fossils behind.

The most famous sites include dinosaur egg and bone beds at Raiyoli in Gujarat and around Dhar in Madhya Pradesh, and Jurassic dinosaurs in the Pranhita–Godavari valley. There are also early whales and [[mammal|mammals]] in Kutch, fossil forests in Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu, and sea shells high in the Himalaya. Many are protected as National Geological Monuments.

options.t: The rocks formed under a sea and were later pushed up as India crashed into Asia

st.reveal: The rocks of the Himalaya include layers of mud that settled on the floor of an ancient ocean, the Tethys. When India collided with Asia, those layers were squeezed and pushed up kilometres into the sky, carrying their fossils with them.

sec.t:
In 1981, [[geologist|geologists]] from the Geological Survey of India were working at a quarry near the village of Raiyoli, in the Balasinor area of Gujarat. They found dinosaur bones and eggs, and the area turned out to be one of the richest dinosaur egg sites anywhere. Bones from Raiyoli later helped describe [[@rajasaurus|Rajasaurus]], a meat-eater with a small horn on its head.

At a nearby site, scientists found a snake fossil curled around a crushed dinosaur egg, next to the bones of a hatchling. The snake, named *Sanajeh*, seems to have been raiding a titanosaur nest when it was suddenly buried by sliding mud and sand. Further east, in Dhar district of Madhya Pradesh, a 2023 study described 92 nesting sites with 256 eggs, some still lying in their clutches.

Much older dinosaurs lie in the Pranhita–Godavari valley, where Telangana and Maharashtra meet. Here scientists dug up [[@barapasaurus|Barapasaurus]], a long-necked plant-eater that lived about 190 million years ago in the early Jurassic. Its name means "big-legged lizard", and it is one of the earliest [[sauropod|sauropods]] known from a large number of bones, dug from the remains of several animals.

{{story:india-drift}}

In Kutch, in western Gujarat, rocks about 40 to 50 million years old hold fossils of early whales that still had legs. They show how [[@whales-walked|whales walked]] on land before returning to the sea. Other early whales of that age are known from Pakistan, then part of the same coastline.

In the Vastan lignite mine near Surat, scientists found [[amber|amber]] about 54 million years old, with insects and spiders trapped inside. The same mine yielded *Cambaytherium*, a small animal related to the ancestors of horses and rhinos, suggesting that this group may have started in India.

Spiti, in Himachal Pradesh, has rocks packed with [[@ammonites|ammonites]], coiled sea shells from creatures related to squid. They lived in the Tethys Ocean, which once lay between India and Asia. When the [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya rose]], the sea floor was pushed high into the sky. In Nepal, smooth black ammonite fossils from the Gandaki river are revered as *shaligrams*.

Along the foothills of the Himalaya, the Siwalik Hills have yielded fossil elephants, rhinos, apes and *Sivatherium*, a giant relative of the giraffe named after Shiva, described in the 1830s.

At Akal near [[@india-wonder-jaisalmer|Jaisalmer]], logs of trees turned to stone lie scattered on the desert ground. They are around 180 million years old, from a time when the Thar was a green coast. At Tiruvakkarai in Tamil Nadu, large fossil tree trunks lie in a protected park. Around Ariyalur, also in Tamil Nadu, Cretaceous sea fossils weather out of the rocks.

Many sites face threats from quarrying and illegal fossil selling. Scientists keep asking for stronger laws, because once a fossil bed is dug up for building stone, the record it held is gone for good.

text: The first woman in space was Valentina Tereshkova, from the Soviet Union. On 16 June 1963, she blasted off alone in a capsule called Vostok 6. She spent nearly three days in [[orbit|orbit]], circling the Earth 48 times, before coming back safely.

She was 26 years old. Before becoming a cosmonaut, as Soviet astronauts were called, she had worked in a [[textile|textile]] factory and made parachute jumps as a hobby. She remains the only woman ever to fly in space completely alone.

The capsule landed gently on wheels
She splashed down in the sea inside the capsule

st.reveal: Vostok capsules landed too hard to be safe for the pilot. So at about 7 km above the ground, the pilot ejected and floated down on a separate parachute, while the capsule came down on its own.

myth: The first woman in space was American.
She was Valentina Tereshkova from the Soviet Union, in 1963. The first American woman in space, Sally Ride, flew 20 years later, in 1983.

sec.h: From the factory floor to the launch pad
sec.t:
Tereshkova grew up in a village near the city of Yaroslavl, northeast of Moscow. Her father was killed in a war when she was a toddler, and her mother worked in a cotton mill. Valentina left school at 16 and went to work in a tyre factory, then the same textile mill.

In her spare time she joined a local parachuting club and made dozens of jumps. That turned out to matter. In the early 1960s, the Soviet space programme decided to send a woman into space, partly to beat the USA to another first. They looked for skilled parachutists, because a Vostok pilot had to eject and parachute to the ground. Out of more than 400 applicants, five women were chosen for training, and Tereshkova was picked to fly.

sec.h: Three days alone above the Earth

sec.t:
The trip home was the scariest part. The Vostok capsule hit the ground too hard for a person to survive comfortably. So at about 7 km above the ground, Tereshkova ejected from her seat and came down under her own [[@parachutes|parachute]].

She landed in a field in the Altai region of Russia, bruised her nose and was greeted by villagers. Reports say she ate the food they offered her, against the rules for returning cosmonauts. Within days, she was a world celebrity.

sec.h: Why it took so long for the next
sec.t:
After Tereshkova, no other woman flew to space for 19 years. The next was Svetlana Savitskaya, also from the Soviet Union, in 1982. She later became the first woman to walk in space. America's first woman astronaut, Sally Ride, flew in 1983.

Since then, about 100 women have flown to space. They include Kalpana Chawla, who in 1997 became the first woman born in India to go to space, and Sunita Williams, who has spent many months aboard the International Space Station. In 2019, NASA astronauts Christina Koch and Jessica Meir made the first spacewalk by two women together.

Tereshkova later became a politician in Russia. Women now command space stations and are training for Moon missions. The full list of their achievements is told in [[@women-in-space|women in space]]. And for a factory worker who learnt to jump from planes for fun, the [[@space-race|space race]] between two superpowers turned a hobby into history. Among the women who followed her was a girl from Karnal who dreamed of flying, [[@kalpana-chawla|Kalpana Chawla]].

text: Most rubbish on beaches doesn't come from boats. It comes from land: blown off streets, washed down drains and rivers, or left behind by visitors. Once it's in the sea, it is very hard to get out again.
Picking it up on the beach catches it at the last step, before waves drag it back in. That helps animals right away. Turtles, seabirds and fish swallow plastic or get tangled in it, and many die.

Beach clean-ups do something else too. Volunteers count what they find. Year after year, those counts tell scientists and governments what kinds of rubbish are reaching the sea and where it is coming from, so they can stop it at the source.

st.reveal: Volunteers counted more than 1.3 million plastic drinks bottles in 2025, with bottle caps also near the top. Cigarette ends topped the list for many earlier years.

myth: A plastic bottle in the sea breaks down and disappears in a few years.
Sunlight and waves break plastic into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics, but it doesn't vanish. Scientists estimate a bottle may take hundreds of years to break down fully.

sec.t:
In October 2015, Afroz Shah, a lawyer in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], moved to a flat overlooking Versova beach. The sand was buried under plastic, in places more than a metre deep. With an elderly neighbour, he started picking it up by hand at weekends.

Fishing families, students and film stars began to join in. Week after week, volunteers hauled away truckloads of waste. In 2016 the United Nations Environment Programme named Shah a Champion of the Earth.

Then, in 2018, Olive Ridley turtle hatchlings were seen scrambling towards the sea at Versova. People who had lived there for years couldn't remember seeing that before. A clean beach had given [[@sea-turtles|sea turtles]] a place to nest again.

The world's biggest clean-up is the International Coastal Cleanup, started by the American group Ocean Conservancy in 1986. Every September, volunteers in more than 100 countries spend a morning on beaches, riverbanks and lake shores.

Since it began, about 20 million people have collected over 405 million pounds of rubbish, about 184 million kilograms. That's heavier than the steel in many big ships.

Every item is logged on a data card or phone app. For years, cigarette ends were the most common thing found. In 2025, plastic drinks bottles topped the list, with bottle caps close behind.

Beach clean-ups are best done in a group with adults. Volunteers wear gloves, carry sacks, and leave anything sharp, like broken glass or needles, for a grown-up with tongs. They also leave shells, seaweed and driftwood where they are, because those belong to the beach. Many groups weigh their sacks at the end, so they can report exactly how much they removed. Some also photograph unusual finds, from toothbrushes to car tyres, to help trace where rubbish comes from.

Sorting what's collected matters too. Some bottles and cans can go to [[@recycling|recycling]]. Old fishing nets can be turned into carpets and clothes.

A clean beach stays clean only if less rubbish arrives. That's why many groups now work along rivers and in towns far from the coast, cleaning drains and creeks. A crisp packet dropped in Pune can travel down rivers and streams for weeks before it reaches the sea. Stop it there, and nobody has to pick it off the sand.

text: No, not really. The Bermuda Triangle is a stretch of the Atlantic Ocean between Miami, the island of Bermuda and Puerto Rico. Stories say ships and planes vanish there without a trace. But when researchers checked the records, they found that disappearances there are no more common than in other busy parts of the ocean.

The real causes of accidents are ordinary, if dangerous: sudden storms, a fast and powerful current, heavy traffic and human mistakes. The "mystery" grew mostly from magazine articles and best-selling books.

Studies by insurers and the US Coast Guard found no extra losses there. It is one of the busiest stretches of ocean in the world, with sudden storms and a fast current, which explains the accidents that do happen.

sec.t:
The name was coined in 1964 by a writer called Vincent Gaddis in a magazine article. In 1974, a book by Charles Berlitz called *The Bermuda Triangle* sold millions of copies. It suggested strange forces, from lost cities to aliens.

The triangle isn't marked on official charts. The US Board on Geographic Names doesn't recognise it. Different writers even draw it in different sizes, from about 1.3 million to nearly 4 million square kilometres. If you're allowed to stretch the borders, more accidents fall inside.

In the 1970s, an American librarian named Lawrence Kusche decided to look up every case himself. He read old newspapers, weather records and official reports.

He found that the stories had been copied from book to book, growing more dramatic each time. Ships said to vanish on calm days had sunk in storms. Some "Bermuda" losses happened in the Pacific, or near Ireland. A few could not be found in any shipping record at all. His 1975 book was titled *The Bermuda Triangle Mystery: Solved*.

sec.h: What makes the sea dangerous there
sec.t:
The [[@ocean-currents|Gulf Stream]] runs through the area. It is one of the strongest currents on Earth, flowing north at up to about 9 km/h. It can push a drifting boat far off course and quickly carry away wreckage.

The region also gets sudden thunderstorms, waterspouts and, from June to November, [[@hurricanes|hurricanes]]. The sea floor drops into some of the deepest trenches in the Atlantic, more than 8 km down, so wrecks can be very hard to find.

Add thousands of ships, cruise liners, fishing boats and small private planes, many flown by amateurs, and some accidents are certain.

You may hear that compasses go haywire there. In parts of the region, a compass needle points close to true north, rather than magnetic north. That's not magic. There are lines like that elsewhere on Earth too, and sailors have known about them for centuries.

Another popular idea is that bubbles of methane gas from the sea floor could sink ships. Scientists have not found evidence that this happens in the Bermuda Triangle.

A good mystery is more fun than a weather report. Once the legend was famous, any accident in the area got linked to it, while accidents elsewhere didn't. That makes the triangle seem deadlier than it is, a trap explained in how [[@statistics-lies|true numbers can mislead]].

NOAA, the US agency that studies the oceans, says plainly that there is no evidence that disappearances there happen more often. Still, the sea does hold real puzzles. The strangest might be the [[@mystery-mary-celeste|Mary Celeste]], found drifting in 1872 in good shape, with every single person gone.

text: A bottle can travel thousands of kilometres, and some have crossed whole oceans. It all depends on the currents it falls into. A bottle doesn't sail. It drifts like a leaf on a stream, carried by [[@ocean-currents|ocean currents]] and pushed a little by the wind.

Some bottles wash up within weeks, a few kilometres away. Others spend years riding huge loops of water that circle each ocean. Many are never found at all. They sink, break on rocks or end up on empty shores where no one walks. The record holder spent 132 years between the throw and the find.

Tides move water in and out along coasts, but the big ocean currents are driven mainly by wind at the surface. Deep down, slow currents are pushed by differences in how cold and salty the water is.

sec.t:
In January 2018, Tonya Illman was walking among the sand dunes near Wedge Island, north of Perth. She found an old, thick glass bottle half buried. Inside was a rolled-up, damp piece of paper.

The Western Australian Museum checked it carefully. The note was a printed form, filled in by hand and dated 12 June 1886. It came from a German sailing ship called the Paula, crossing the Indian Ocean. The German Naval Observatory had asked ships to throw bottles overboard, each with a form asking the finder to report where it landed. Over about 69 years, thousands of bottles were thrown, and a few hundred forms came back. This one was the last to be found.

Ocean currents are like rivers running through the sea. Winds push the surface water, and the turning of the Earth bends its path. Together they make giant loops called [[gyre|gyres]], which circle the middle of each big ocean.

The Gulf Stream is one of the fastest currents. It runs up the east coast of the United States and across the Atlantic. In places it flows at up to about 9 km/h, faster than you can walk. A bottle caught in it could reach Europe within a year or so.

The Indian Ocean is unusual. In the north, its currents change direction with the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. In summer they flow one way around India and in winter they turn back. Sailors trading between India, Arabia and East Africa used those seasonal flips for centuries.

{{story:monsoon}}

In January 1992, a storm in the North Pacific knocked shipping containers off a cargo ship. One held about 29,000 plastic bath toys: yellow ducks, blue turtles, red beavers and green frogs.

The toys floated off in a crowd. Months later some washed up on the coast of Alaska. Others spent years drifting around the North Pacific gyre. An American oceanographer, Curtis Ebbesmeyer, asked beachcombers to report every toy they found. Their reports helped scientists test computer models of how currents move. The story became a children's book and made the ducks famous.

Today, scientists don't need to wait for strangers to find bottles. About 4,000 robot floats, part of a project called Argo, drift through the oceans as of 2025. Every ten days or so, each one sinks to about 2,000 m, measures temperature and saltiness, then rises and beams its data to a satellite. India runs some of them in the Indian Ocean.

Satellites also track buoys on the surface using [[@gps-how|GPS]]. In one day they send back more information than all the old bottle experiments put together.

sec.h: Not such a good idea now
sec.t:
Throwing a bottle into the sea once felt romantic. Now we know how much rubbish ends up in the oceans, and a glass or [[@ocean-plastic|plastic]] bottle is one more piece of it. Many beach-cleaning groups ask people to keep their messages on land.

The bottles that do turn up still tell a story. Each one is a record of a long, slow journey that nobody watched.

text: A sewing machine joins cloth with two threads instead of one. The top thread runs from a spool down to the needle. The bottom thread sits on a tiny reel called a bobbin, under the cloth.

Each time the needle stabs down, it carries a loop of top thread just below the fabric. A spinning hook grabs that loop and swings it around the bobbin, wrapping it around the bottom thread. Then the needle rises, a [[lever|lever]] pulls the top thread tight, and the two threads lock together in the middle of the cloth. This is called a lockstitch. A home machine can make several hundred of them a minute.

st.prompt: On a sewing machine needle, where is the hole that the thread goes through?

At the blunt top, like a hand needle
In the middle

st.reveal: The needle only dips a short way through the cloth and comes back up. With the hole near the tip, it can push a loop of thread underneath for a hook to grab. A hand needle has to travel all the way through, so its hole is at the back.

myth: A sewing machine just copies hand sewing very quickly, with one needle and one thread going in and out.

A hand stitch uses one thread that passes right through the cloth. The common machine stitch uses two threads, one above and one below, that twist together inside the cloth. Inventors only succeeded once they stopped trying to copy a human hand.

sec.t:
The parts move together like a team of [[@gears|gears]] and levers, all driven by one turning shaft. As the needle reaches its lowest point and starts to rise, [[friction|friction]] in the cloth holds back a little of the thread. That makes a small loop beside the needle.

A pointed hook spins past and snags it. Some machines use a hook that whirls in a circle, others a shuttle that rocks back and forth. Either way, the loop is pulled wide and slipped around the bobbin case. Below the needle, small metal teeth called feed dogs grip the cloth and push it forward by one stitch length. Then everything repeats.

Turn the stitch-length dial and the feed dogs push the cloth further each time. For a zigzag stitch, the needle swings from side to side between stitches. Zigzags stretch with the fabric and stop cut edges from fraying.

Early machines were expensive. Singer's company let families pay a little each month instead of all at once, one of the first big uses of this kind of hire purchase. By the late 1800s, sewing machines were among the most common machines in homes around the world.

In India, the treadle machine, worked by rocking a foot plate, became the tool of the neighbourhood darzi, or tailor. A company in Kolkata began making sewing machines under the name Usha in the 1930s. Many tailors still work on foot-powered machines because they need no electricity and can be repaired almost anywhere.

Most clothes you wear were stitched on industrial machines. Some make 5,000 or more stitches a minute, so fast that the needle is a blur. Special machines sew buttonholes, attach buttons or trim and bind the edge of fabric at the same time.

A T-shirt might pass through several machines, each run by a different worker. Garment hubs like Tiruppur in Tamil Nadu, and factories in Bangladesh, China and Vietnam, sew clothes for shops across the world. A pair of [[@jeans|jeans]] can have over a dozen separate seams, and each one is held together by the same loop-and-hook trick.

text: The harmonium is a small box with a keyboard on top and bellows at the back. You pump the bellows with one hand and play the keys with the other. It came to India from Europe in the 1800s, during British rule, and Indian musicians quickly made it their own.
It caught on for practical reasons. It is easy to carry, it stays in tune for years, and a beginner can play a melody within days. Singers love it because it gives them a steady note to sing against.

options.t: Thin metal reeds shaken by air
Strings hit by small hammers
Pipes like a church organ

st.reveal: Each key opens a hole under a thin brass reed. Air pushed by the bellows rushes past and makes the reed vibrate hundreds of times a second. A mouth organ works the same way, with your breath as the bellows.

d.try: Hold a blade of grass or a thin strip of paper tightly between your two thumbs and blow hard across the gap. The buzzing you hear is a reed vibrating in moving air, the same idea that makes a harmonium sing.
myth: The harmonium is an ancient Indian instrument.

It was invented in Europe in the 19th century and reached India during British rule. Indian makers then changed it so much, with hand bellows and a small floor-sitting body, that it now feels completely Indian.

sec.t:
Inside a harmonium are rows of thin brass tongues called reeds, each fixed over a slot. When you press a key, a hole opens. Air from the bellows rushes through and makes that reed wobble, producing one note. Short reeds give high notes and long reeds give low ones.

This kind of reed is called a free reed, and it is very old. China's *sheng*, a mouth organ of [[@bamboo|bamboo]] pipes, has used free reeds for thousands of years. European inventors borrowed the idea in the 1700s and 1800s. In 1840, Alexandre Debain in Paris patented an instrument he called the harmonium.

Many harmoniums have knobs called stops. Pulling one lets air reach an extra set of reeds, which makes the sound fuller. Some Indian models also have a scale changer: the whole keyboard slides sideways, so a singer can move every note higher or lower to suit their voice without learning new fingering.

Not everyone was pleased. Rabindranath [[@tagore|Tagore]] disliked it, and so did John Foulds, a British composer who worked at [[@radio-india|All India Radio]] in the 1930s. Their main complaint was about tuning. Indian music often glides smoothly from one note to another, a slide called *meend*, and it uses tiny shades of pitch. A harmonium can only jump from key to key, with each note fixed.

In 1940, All India Radio stopped using the harmonium on air. The ban lasted until 1971. During those years, musicians kept using it everywhere else, on stage, in films and in homes.

Today you can hear a harmonium in a village bhajan, a [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] song or a classical concert. Sikh ragis play it while singing kirtan at the Golden Temple in [[@amritsar|Amritsar]]. Masters like Pandit Tulsidas Borkar and Pandit Appasaheb Jalgaonkar showed that, in skilled hands, it can be a solo instrument too.

The old argument has not completely gone away. Some musicians still prefer the sarangi, a bowed string instrument that can slide between notes. But the harmonium is cheap, sturdy and forgiving. It also travelled with Indian families abroad, so you can hear it in gurdwaras and temples in Canada, Britain and the United States. For millions of children, its keys are where learning music begins.

text: Madhubani painting is a folk art from the Mithila region of [[@bihar-history|northern Bihar]] and southern [[@nepal|Nepal]]. It is named after the district of Madhubani, one of its main centres. The paintings are full of bold outlines, bright colours and patterns that fill every bit of space.

For centuries, women painted these pictures on the freshly plastered mud walls and floors of their homes. They painted for festivals, for prayers and especially for [[@life-weddings-world|weddings]]. The pictures show gods and goddesses, scenes from the epics, and symbols of nature such as fish, peacocks, the sun, the moon and trees.

sec.t:
One of the most important places for Madhubani painting was the *kohbar ghar*, the room where a newly married couple would stay. Women covered its walls with paintings full of symbols of love, long life and children.

Fish stood for good luck and fertility. Parrots and peacocks stood for love. [[@bamboo|Bamboo]] and [[@lotus|lotus]] plants, painted together, stood for the couple. Mothers taught daughters, and each family had its own favourite designs. Many paintings show stories from the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]]. Sita, the heroine, is said to have come from Mithila, and her wedding to Rama is a favourite scene.

sec.t:
In January 1934, a powerful [[@earthquakes|earthquake]] struck Bihar and Nepal. A British official named William G. Archer was sent to inspect the damage around Madhubani. In the broken houses, he saw that the inner walls were covered with paintings.

Archer photographed them and, in 1949, wrote an article about them in the Indian art magazine *Marg*. For the first time, people outside Mithila began to take notice.

In the mid-1960s, a severe [[@droughts|drought]] hit Bihar. Crops failed and families went hungry. The All India Handicrafts Board sent the artist Bhaskar Kulkarni to Mithila to encourage women to paint on paper, so their work could be sold.

It worked. Women who had only ever painted at home began selling their paintings across India and abroad. Some became famous, and painters began to sign their work and sell it in city exhibitions. In 1975, Jagdamba Devi became the first Madhubani artist to receive the Padma Shri, one of India's top civilian honours. Sita Devi and Ganga Devi also became well known.

Madhubani is often divided into styles, such as *bharni*, which fills shapes with solid colour, and *kachni*, which uses fine lines. Artists from different communities added their own styles, such as *godna*, inspired by tattoo designs.

In 2007, Madhubani painting received a Geographical Indication tag, which protects its name as an art from that region. Today, you can find it on saris, bags and even the walls of Madhubani railway station. It belongs to a family of Indian folk arts, alongside [[@warli|Warli painting]] from Maharashtra.

text: Economics is the study of how people, families, companies and countries decide what to do with things that are limited. There is only so much money, so much land, so much water and so many hours in a day. Wanting is easy. Having enough of everything is impossible.

So everyone must choose. Should a family spend its savings on a scooter or on school fees? Should a farmer grow rice or cotton? Should a government build a new road or a new hospital? Economists study how those choices are made, what happens because of them, and whether there might be a better way.

sec.t:
The most useful idea in economics is called opportunity cost. Every time you choose something, you give up the next best thing you could have had instead.

If you spend your last ₹100 on a book, the cost is the cricket ball you didn't buy. If you spend Saturday at a friend's house, the cost is the film you skipped. The idea works for whole countries too. Money spent on army tanks is money not spent on schools. Seeing that hidden cost helps people choose more carefully.

Economists often split their subject into two halves. Microeconomics looks closely at single choices: why a shop sets a price, why a family buys one brand of soap and not another, why a worker takes one job. Ideas such as [[@supply-demand|supply and demand]] belong here.

Macroeconomics zooms out to a whole country. It asks why prices rise over time, called [[@inflation|inflation]], why some years have more jobs than others, and how much a government should borrow. It also measures the size of whole [[economy|economies]], usually with GDP, the total value of everything a country produces in a year. That is how we know the USA and China have the two largest. Central banks, like the Reserve Bank of India and the US Federal Reserve, use macroeconomics to set interest rates.

Economists also study choices that look odd. Why do people buy things they don't need just because there's a sale? Why do they keep paying for a gym they never visit? A newer branch called behavioural economics mixes economics with psychology to explain why real people don't always act the way a textbook says they should.

{{story:game-theory}}

People thought about these questions long before the word economics existed. The Arthashastra, an ancient Indian book on running a kingdom, is linked to [[@chanakya|Chanakya]], adviser to the Mauryan emperor. It discusses [[@taxes|taxes]], trade, prices and workers' wages. Scholars still argue about exactly when it was written and by whom.

In Scotland in 1776, Adam Smith wrote The Wealth of Nations. He described a pin workshop where each worker did one small step, and together they made thousands of pins a day. He also argued that when people trade freely, each looking after their own interest, the whole society can end up better off.

Economics is about people, and people are hard to predict. Two economists can look at the same numbers and disagree about what to do. Should a government spend more in hard times, or save? Do high taxes on the rich help everyone, or slow things down? These arguments are often in the news.

Some economists study things that seem far from money. The Indian economist Amartya Sen won the Nobel Prize in economics in 1998. Part of his work showed that [[famine|famines]] can happen even when a country has enough food, because poor people cannot afford to buy it. That idea changed how governments respond to hunger, and it began with a simple question about who gets what.

text: An average is one number that tries to sum up a whole group of numbers. The trouble is that there are several kinds, and they can give very different answers.

The **mean** is what most people call "the average". Add all the numbers and divide by how many there are. The **median** is the middle number when you line them all up in order. The **mode** is the number that turns up most often.

For many groups, like the heights of children in a class, all three come out close together. But when a few numbers are very big or very small, they can split far apart. Choosing which average to use can change the story completely.

sec.h: Why the mean can fool you
sec.t:
Suppose ten people in a room each earn ₹30,000 a month. The mean is ₹30,000. Now a billionaire walks in. The mean suddenly shoots up to many crores, but nobody else in the room got any richer.

The median hardly changes. The middle person in the line is still earning ₹30,000. That is why reports about money often use the median income. It tells you more about a typical person.

The mode is useful in different ways. A shoe shop cares about which size sells most, not the mean shoe size. Nobody wants a shoe in size 7.3.

In the late 1940s, the US Air Force had a problem. Too many pilots were losing control of their planes, and the machines themselves weren't faulty. Cockpits had been built to fit the average pilot of the 1920s.

A researcher named Gilbert Daniels measured about 4,000 pilots on ten body sizes, such as arm length, chest and leg length. Then he checked how many were close to average on all ten. The answer was none.

The Air Force changed course. Cockpits got adjustable seats, pedals and straps that could fit a wide range of bodies. Car seats and office chairs that slide and tilt come from the same idea. Nobody is average at everything, so good design has to bend.

[[@weather-forecasts|Weather forecasts]] talk about "average rainfall" for a month. Doctors compare a child's height and weight with averages to check they are growing well, while knowing healthy children come in many sizes. A school report might show your class's average mark next to yours.

An average is a useful shortcut. It just leaves out a lot. Two classes can have the same mean score, yet in one everyone scored about the same, and in the other half scored very high and half very low. To see the whole story, you also need to know how spread out the numbers are, and a good [[@graphs-charts|chart]] often shows that best.

text: Roman numerals use seven letters to stand for numbers. I is 1, V is 5, X is 10, L is 50, C is 100, D is 500 and M is 1,000. To write a number, add letters together, starting with the biggest. So XVII is 10 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 17.

There is one twist. When a smaller letter comes before a bigger one, you subtract it. IV is 5 minus 1, which is 4, and XC is 100 minus 10, which is 90. The Romans had no zero, which made big sums hard. That is why these numerals faded from everyday use, but you can still spot them on clocks, buildings and film credits.

Romans often wrote IIII and VIIII. The rule of putting a smaller numeral before a larger one to subtract was used, but it became standard mainly in the Middle Ages and later. Clocks showing IIII are following an old habit, not making a mistake.

sec.t:
The Roman system grew out of tally marks, the scratches people make when keeping count. One stroke, I, was one. Many historians think V for five may come from the shape of an open hand, with the thumb and fingers spread, and that X looks like two Vs joined point to point. Over time the symbols came to look like Latin letters.

[[@ancient-rome|Ancient Rome]] borrowed ideas from the Etruscans, who lived in Italy before the Romans grew powerful. The Etruscans used similar marks. Around the [[empire|empire]], from Britain to Egypt, the same numerals appeared on coins, milestones, buildings and tombstones.

Try adding CXXIII and XLIX in your head. It is not easy. The Romans did not do sums with numerals. They used counting boards and a kind of [[@abacus|abacus]] with pebbles in grooves. The Latin word for pebble, calculus, gives us the English words "calculate" and "calculus".

Roman numerals have no zero and no [[@place-value|place value]]. In our system, the 2 in 200 means something different from the 2 in 20. In Roman numerals, X always means ten, wherever it sits. That makes long multiplication almost impossible. When Indian digits with zero reached Europe in the Middle Ages, merchants slowly switched over, though some cities resisted for a long time.

At the [[@colosseum|Colosseum]] in Rome, the arches around the outside were numbered so crowds could find their seats. You can still read LII, 52, above one of them.

Today Roman numerals often appear where something should look grand or old-fashioned. They label kings and queens, like Elizabeth II, as well as book chapters, the copyright dates at the end of films and many [[@clocks|clock]] faces. The [[@super-bowl|Super Bowl]], the final of [[@american-football|American football]], is numbered in Roman numerals. In 2016 the organisers made one exception and called it Super Bowl 50 instead of Super Bowl L, because they thought a lone L looked odd. In India, you may see them on old buildings from British times and on some school certificates.

text: [[@maths-snowflakes|Snowflakes are six-sided]] because [[@earth-weird-frost-flowers|ice crystals]] are six-sided, the same reason ice floats.

A water [[molecule|molecule]] is shaped a bit like a boomerang: one oxygen [[atom|atom]] with two hydrogen atoms sticking out at an angle. When water freezes, the molecules link up in rings of six, making a honeycomb-like pattern. A tiny ice crystal therefore starts life as a flat hexagon, and arms sprout from its six corners.
The shape of the arms depends on the temperature and wetness of the air the flake falls through.

frames.cap: High in a freezing cloud, water vapour sticks to a speck of dust.

Each flake takes its own path through the cloud, so no two end up exactly the same.

sec.t:
Snowflakes begin high in a cloud, where the air is below freezing. Water vapour, the invisible gas form of water, settles onto a speck of dust and turns straight into ice. More vapour keeps arriving and freezing, so the crystal grows.

The corners of the hexagon stick out a little further into the damp air, so they catch vapour faster and grow into arms. All six arms sit in the same air at the same moment, so they grow almost alike. That is why the result has [[@symmetry|symmetry]], even though no part of the flake "knows" what the others are doing.

Wilson Bentley grew up on a farm in Jericho, Vermont, in the USA. On 15 January 1885, aged 19, he became the first person known to photograph a single snowflake, by fixing a camera to a [[microscope|microscope]]. He caught flakes on a black board and worked fast in the cold before they melted or his breath spoiled them.

Bentley photographed about 5,000 snowflakes over 40 years and never found two alike. In 1931, a book of his pictures came out, and he died later that year.

Most snowflakes have six arms, but nature sometimes bends the rule. Scientists who photograph snow crystals have found rare three-sided flakes, and even twelve-armed ones, made when two six-armed crystals grow stuck together at a twist.

Many snowflakes are also lopsided, because one arm hit a different patch of air or bumped into another flake. And plenty of snow falls as broken bits, clumps or tiny columns that look nothing like the perfect stars on greeting cards. The neat six-armed star is real, but it is only one member of a big, untidy family.

A large snowflake contains many billions of water molecules, and each takes a slightly different path through the cloud. The chances of two complex flakes matching exactly are so tiny that scientists treat it as impossible.

Very simple crystals are another matter. In 1988, a scientist named Nancy Knight found two tiny crystals from a storm cloud over the USA that looked the same under a microscope. In India, you can see snowflakes for yourself in winter in places like Gulmarg, Shimla and [[@ladakh|Ladakh]]. The rules are the same as in a freezer: [[@why-ice-floats|ice]] builds in sixes, and [[@snow-hail|snow]] records the weather on its way down.

George Harrison had already fallen in love with Indian music. Through him, millions of young people around the world heard the sitar for the first time. Their trip to Rishikesh made many people curious about India, yoga and meditation.

sec.h: A sitar on a pop record
sec.t:
In 1965, during a film shoot, Harrison picked up a sitar that was lying around the set. He taught himself enough to play a tune on the Beatles' song "Norwegian Wood". It was one of the first times millions of pop fans heard one.

He wanted to learn properly. In 1966 he travelled to India to study with the great sitar player [[@ravi-shankar|Ravi Shankar]], who told him that mastering the instrument takes many years. Harrison never became a concert sitarist, but he kept bringing Indian instruments and ideas into Beatles songs, such as "Within You Without You" in 1967.

With no TV, no concerts and no fans outside, the Beatles had time to write. They sat on rooftops and verandas with acoustic guitars, and Donovan taught Lennon and McCartney a new way of picking the strings. In a few weeks they wrote around 40 songs.

Many ended up on their next album, simply called *The Beatles* but known as the "White Album" for its plain white cover, released in November 1968. Others appeared later on other records.

The group left at different times. Ringo Starr went home first. Lennon and Harrison stayed until April, leaving after a falling-out with the Maharishi, whose details are still disputed.

In the 1960s, many young people in Europe and America became curious about Indian music, yoga and [[philosophy|philosophy]]. The Beatles' interest made that curiosity even bigger. Ravi Shankar played sitar at huge Western [[@festivals-music|music festivals]], including Woodstock in 1969, and taught many musicians.

In 1971, Harrison and Shankar organised the Concert for [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]] in New York, to raise money for [[refugee|refugees]] from war in what is now Bangladesh. It was one of the first big charity concerts of its kind. Shankar helped make Indian classical music and its [[@raga-time|ragas]] famous around the world.

After the Maharishi left, the ashram was abandoned and the forest grew back over it. It now lies inside Rajaji Tiger Reserve, and was opened to visitors in 2015. Artists have covered its crumbling walls with [[mural|murals]] of the band and of Indian gods. Below it, the Ganga still flows out of the [[@rivers-himalaya|Himalaya]], cold and fast, as it did in 1968.

text: Bollywood is the Hindi-language film industry based in Mumbai. It began in 1913, when a printer and photographer named Dhundiraj Govind Phalke, later known as [[@dadasaheb-phalke|Dadasaheb Phalke]], made *Raja Harishchandra*, India's first full-length feature film. It was silent and in black and white, and it told a story from Indian [[mythology|mythology]].

The name "Bollywood" came much later. It mixes Bombay, the old name of [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], with Hollywood, and it became common in the 1970s. Today the industry makes hundreds of films a year and is watched from Lagos to London.

Bollywood is the Hindi film industry based in Mumbai. India also has huge film industries in Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, Bengali, Marathi and other languages, and together they make far more films than Bollywood alone.

sec.h: A man who pawned his wife's jewellery

sec.t:
For almost 20 years, Indian films were silent. Then in 1931 came *Alam Ara*, directed by Ardeshir Irani, India's first "talkie", or film with sound. It had seven songs. Audiences loved them, and [[@film-songs|film songs]] have been part of Hindi cinema ever since.

Sound changed everything. Films now had to choose a language, and Bombay's studios settled on Hindustani, a mix of Hindi and Urdu understood across much of north India. Other cities, such as Madras and Calcutta, built strong film industries in Tamil, Telugu and Bengali.

The 1950s and 1960s are often called Hindi cinema's golden age. Directors such as [[@raj-kapoor|Raj Kapoor]], Guru Dutt and Bimal Roy made films about poverty, love and a newly independent country. *[[@bollywood-classics|Mother India]]* (1957) was nominated for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film. Playback singers such as [[@lata-mangeshkar|Lata Mangeshkar]] recorded the songs, while actors moved their lips on screen.

In 1975 came *Sholay*, an action film set in a dusty village. It ran in one Bombay cinema, Minerva, for about five years without a break.

sec.h: How a Bollywood film is made today
sec.t:
A big Bollywood film looks very different from Phalke's. It may be shot in [[@switzerland|Switzerland]], London and [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], with crews of hundreds. The songs are often recorded before filming, so dancers can perform to the music. Computers add [[@special-effects|special effects]], and [[@dubbing-subtitles|dubbing]] artists may record new voices in Tamil or Telugu for release in other states.

Many studios and sets are at Film City in Goregaon, a large stretch of land on the edge of Sanjay Gandhi National Park, in north Mumbai. Leopards have occasionally wandered onto the sets.

The Government of India's highest award for cinema, started in 1969, is named the Dadasaheb Phalke Award. Phalke himself made more than 90 films, but he died in 1944, poor and largely forgotten, just as talkies had made his silent style old-fashioned. Many of his films have been lost. The fragments that survive are looked after by the National Film Archive of India in Pune.

text: Most healthy people can hold their breath for somewhere between 30 seconds and about a minute and a half. Trained freedivers, who practise for years under careful supervision, can go much longer. The longest breath-holds on ordinary air recorded in competition are close to 12 minutes.

With a special trick, breathing pure oxygen for several minutes first, the Croatian freediver Vitomir Maričić held his breath for 29 minutes and 3 seconds in 2025, a Guinness world record. That is about the time it takes to bake a tray of biscuits. Records like these are set with safety divers watching every second. Doctors check the divers before and after, because the body is being pushed close to its limits.

st.prompt: When you hold your breath, what makes you feel you must breathe?

options.t: Carbon dioxide building up in your blood
Your lungs running completely out of oxygen
Your heart stopping for a moment

st.reveal: Sensors in your brain and blood vessels track carbon dioxide, the waste gas you breathe out. As it rises, your brain sends stronger and stronger signals to breathe. You still have plenty of oxygen left when the urge starts.

d.try: Sit still and count how many breaths you take in one minute. Then do 30 star jumps and count again. Your body breathes faster to clear the extra carbon dioxide your muscles made. Don't do breath-holding contests, especially in water.
myth: Taking lots of fast, deep breaths before going underwater lets you stay down safely for longer.
Fast breathing lowers carbon dioxide, so the warning signal to breathe comes later, but your oxygen doesn't rise much. Swimmers can black out without warning. Never practise breath-holding in water.

sec.t:
Humans have an old reflex that we share with seals and whales. When cold water touches your face, your heart slows down. Blood vessels in your arms and legs tighten, saving oxygen for the brain and heart. This is called the mammalian dive reflex.

Your spleen, an organ tucked under your left ribs, helps too. It stores spare red blood cells and squeezes them out during a long dive, adding more oxygen-carrying cells to your blood.

The Bajau people of Southeast Asia have lived on boats and coasts for centuries, diving for fish and shellfish, some in the waters of [[@world-indonesia|Indonesia]]. Some divers spend hours a day underwater, on single breaths, reaching depths of 70 m.

A 2018 study found that Bajau people have spleens about 50 percent larger than their land-farming neighbours, and that [[gene|genes]] linked to this have become common among them. It is a rare example of humans [[evolve|evolving]] to suit a way of life in recent history. In Korea and Japan, women divers called haenyeo and ama have worked the sea in a similar way for generations.

Compared with sea [[mammal|mammals]], our best is tiny. Sperm whales dive for over an hour. In 2020 scientists reported a Cuvier's beaked whale that stayed under for 222 minutes, almost four hours. Seals and whales store huge amounts of oxygen in their muscles, using a [[protein|protein]] that makes the muscles look almost black.

Even an emperor penguin can stay down for over 20 minutes. Sea turtles resting on the seabed in cold water can go for hours, because their bodies use oxygen so slowly. Some freshwater turtles survive whole winters under ice, taking in a little oxygen through their skin.

The other way to test your oxygen supply is to go up. At the top of Everest, each breath holds only about a third of the oxygen it would at sea level. Climbers breathe fast and deep just to cope, which is the strange world of [[@altitude|altitude]].

Your own breath-holding record matters much less than knowing how your [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] and brain work together. They keep you breathing every few seconds for your whole life, including all night, without you ever having to remember.

text: Hunger is a message from your body to your brain saying "time to refuel". Several signals work together. Your stomach releases a [[hormone|hormone]] called ghrelin when it has been empty for a while, and ghrelin travels in the blood to the brain. Your blood sugar levels, your fat stores and even your daily routine add their own signals.

All this information arrives at the hypothalamus, a small area deep in the brain. It weighs the "eat now" signals against "I'm full" signals and creates the feeling we call hunger. Once you eat, the stomach stretches and the gut releases other hormones that tell your brain to stop.

st.prompt: Before your usual lunchtime, levels of the hunger hormone ghrelin often rise in your blood. What seems to set them off?

options.t: Your body's habit of eating at that time
The sound of other people eating

st.reveal: Ghrelin tends to rise before regular mealtimes, as if the body is getting ready for food it expects. That's partly why you feel hungry at your usual lunch hour even if you had a big breakfast.

myth: Your stomach shrinks if you eat less, so you'll stop feeling hungry.
An adult stomach doesn't permanently shrink from eating less. Feelings of hunger come mostly from hormones and the brain, not just from how big or empty the stomach is.

Time for fullness signals to build
often said to be about 20 minutes

sec.t:
In the early 1900s, the American physiologist Walter Cannon wanted to know whether hunger came from the stomach. His student Arthur Washburn trained himself to swallow a small balloon attached to a tube. Once it was in his stomach, the balloon was blown up a little, and any squeeze of the stomach pushed air up the tube to a recording device.

Washburn pressed a key each time he felt a hunger pang. The pangs matched the stomach's squeezes. In 1912, they published their results. Later scientists found that people whose stomachs had been removed still felt hungry, so the stomach can't be the whole story.

Two discoveries in the 1990s changed the picture. In 1994, Jeffrey Friedman's team in New York found leptin, a hormone made by fat cells. The more fat the body stores, the more leptin it releases, telling the brain there is energy to spare.

In 1999, Japanese scientists Masayasu Kojima and Kenji Kangawa discovered ghrelin. It rises when the stomach is empty and before regular mealtimes, and falls after eating. It's the main hormone that says "eat".

When you start eating, the stretching stomach and intestines release fullness hormones. These signals take a little time to build, which is one reason why eating slowly can help you notice when you've had enough.

{{story:mid-day-meal}}

Every couple of hours on an empty stomach, waves of muscle squeezes sweep through your stomach and intestines, pushing leftover bits along. [[@stomach-growl|Gas and liquid gurgle]] as they're squeezed. With food inside, the noise is muffled. With no food, it echoes, and everyone in the classroom hears it.

Rumbling doesn't always mean you're hungry, and you can be hungry without rumbling. The sound is a clue, not a reliable signal.

Hunger is your body needing food. Appetite is wanting food, and it can be switched on by smell, sight and habit. The smell of fresh jalebis or popcorn can make you want to eat even straight after dinner. Around 1900, the Russian scientist Ivan Pavlov showed that dogs started to drool at signals that meant food was coming.

Foods packed with sugar, salt and fat, like many types of [[@junk-food|junk food]], can be easy to keep eating even when you're full. Lack of [[@sleep-why|sleep]] can also push up hunger hormones.

Feeling hungry before a meal is normal. Going hungry for long periods is not. Children who don't get enough to eat find it harder to concentrate and grow. That is why programmes such as India's [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal scheme]] and school lunch programmes in the USA provide food for millions of children every school day.

text: A baby's mouth and jaw are small, so they can only fit small teeth. Children grow a first set of 20 baby teeth, also called milk teeth. As your face and jaw grow, there's room for bigger, stronger teeth, and more of them.

Your adult teeth have been forming inside your jaw since you were very young. When one is ready, it pushes up against the baby tooth above it. Your body slowly [[dissolve|dissolves]] the baby tooth's root. With no root to hold it, the baby tooth gets wobbly and falls out, and the adult tooth moves into the gap.
Most children [[@life-tooth-fairy|start losing teeth]] around age 6 or 7, usually the bottom front ones first, and finish by about 12.

options.t: No, they are a different kind of tissue
Yes, they are the hardest bones

st.reveal: Teeth are not bones. Bones can heal themselves when they break, but the enamel on a tooth can't regrow. Teeth are made of enamel, a softer layer called dentine, and a living centre called the pulp.

d.try: Look in a mirror and count your teeth, top and bottom. Compare the number with the 20 baby teeth and 32 adult teeth a full set can have. Ask an adult in your family how many teeth they have, and whether they remember losing their first one.
myth: Baby teeth don't matter, because they fall out anyway.
Baby teeth help children chew, speak clearly and keep space in the jaw for the adult teeth. Badly decayed baby teeth can cause pain and infection, so they need brushing just as much as adult ones.

sec.t:
Humans get only two sets of teeth. Baby teeth start growing before birth, hidden in the gums, and the first one usually appears at about six months. All 20 are in by about age three.

A full adult set has 32 teeth. The last four, called wisdom teeth, often don't appear until the late teens or twenties. Some people never get them, and some have them removed because there isn't room.

Once your adult teeth are in, that's it. If one is lost, it won't grow back. Dentists can fill the gap with an artificial tooth, but your body can't make a third set.

Some animals have far more chances than we do. [[@sharks-old|Sharks]] grow row after row of teeth. When one falls out, the one behind moves forward, and a shark may get through thousands in its life.

Elephants take another route. They get six sets of big grinding molars, one after another, moving forward along the jaw like a slow conveyor belt. When the last set wears down, usually in old age, an elephant finds it hard to chew. An [[@elephants-talk|elephant's]] tusks are teeth too: they are giant front teeth that keep growing.

People around the world have traditions for lost baby teeth. In the USA, Britain and Canada, many children put a tooth under their pillow for the Tooth Fairy, who may leave a coin. In many parts of India, children throw the tooth onto the roof, sometimes asking a sparrow or crow to bring a strong new one. In Spain and Latin America, a little mouse called Ratoncito Pérez collects it.

All these customs mark the same moment: a small step in growing up.

Because teeth appear in a fairly fixed order, dentists can estimate a child's age from an [[@x-rays|X-ray]] of their jaw. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] do the same with ancient skulls. Teeth are so tough that they are often the best-preserved part of a skeleton, sometimes lasting hundreds of thousands of years.

text: Many great cities were abandoned over time and then forgotten by most of the world. Some were swallowed by forests, like Maya cities in Central America. Others were buried by sand or soil, like Mohenjo-daro in the Indus valley, or by a volcano, like [[@pompeii|Pompeii]] in Italy. Wars destroyed some, like Hampi in India.

Centuries later, travellers, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] and sometimes farmers found them again. The word "lost" can mislead, though. Local people often knew the ruins well. What was lost was the wider world's memory of them, and often the city's own history.

sec.t:
High in the Andes mountains of Peru, the Inca built Machu Picchu around 1450, probably as an estate for an emperor. When Spanish invaders conquered the Inca in the 1500s, they never found it, so its stone buildings survived.

In 1911, Hiram Bingham, a lecturer from Yale University, was led there by local people. His photos in *National Geographic* made it world-famous. Today it is one of the most visited sites in South America, and Peru limits visitor numbers to protect it.

For thousands of years, Mohenjo-daro lay under mounds in Sindh, now in Pakistan. In the 1920s, archaeologists, including R.D. Banerji of the Archaeological Survey of India, began digging. They found a planned city of baked brick with straight streets, a great bath and covered drains.

It was part of the [[@indus-cities|Indus civilisation]], about 4,500 years old. Before these digs, nobody knew that people in South Asia had built such cities so early. Their writing has still not been deciphered.

[[@hampi|Hampi]], in Karnataka, was the capital of the [[@vijayanagara|Vijayanagara]] [[empire|empire]]. In the 1400s and 1500s, visitors from Persia and Portugal described huge markets selling rubies, horses and spices. After a defeat in battle in 1565, the city was looted and abandoned.

Hampi was never fully forgotten. Its Virupaksha temple has stayed in worship. But its palaces and bazaars fell into ruin among giant boulders. Today it is a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site.

Ancient Greek poems told of Troy, a city besieged in a great war. Many thought it was only a story. In the 1870s, Heinrich Schliemann dug at a mound called Hisarlik in Turkey and found layers of ruined cities, one on top of another. Most archaeologists now accept it was Troy, though Schliemann's rough digging destroyed a lot of evidence.

In Jordan, the rock-carved city of [[@petra|Petra]] was home to local Bedouin people. In 1812 a Swiss traveller, Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, disguised himself to visit it and told Europe about it.

Some lost cities may still be out there, under forests, deserts or the sea, waiting for the right tool or a lucky farmer.

text: Some of the world's most valuable objects are missing, and no one knows exactly where they are. The Amber Room, a room in a Russian palace lined with golden amber panels, disappeared during the Second World War. The Peacock Throne, made for the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, was carried off from Delhi in 1739 and later broken up. A Portuguese ship called the *Flor de la Mar* sank in 1511 with a hold full of treasure, and its wreck has never been confirmed.

Others are lost in a different way. Some royal eggs made by the jeweller Fabergé are still unaccounted for. And in 2025, thieves walked out of the Louvre in Paris with eight pieces of French crown jewellery that police have still not found.

A kind of orange glass made in Russia
A stone that forms near volcanoes

st.reveal: Amber is fossilised tree resin, the sticky stuff that oozes from pine trees. Over millions of years it hardens into a glowing, golden material. The Amber Room used about six tonnes of it.

sec.t:
The Amber Room was made in Prussia, in what is now Germany, in the early 1700s. In 1716, the Prussian king gave it to Peter the Great of Russia. It ended up in the Catherine Palace near St Petersburg, its walls glowing with about six tonnes of [[amber|amber]], gold leaf and mirrors.

In 1941, invading German soldiers took the room apart in about 36 hours, packed it into crates and shipped it to the city of Königsberg. In 1945, as the war ended, the trail goes cold. It may have burned in a fire. It may be hidden in a mine or a bunker. Treasure hunters are still searching. Russian craftsmen spent more than 20 years building a copy, which opened in 2003.

sec.h: The ship with an emperor's fortune
sec.t: The *Flor de la Mar* was a Portuguese ship. In 1511, it sailed from Malacca, in today's Malaysia, carrying riches taken from the city's sultan. A storm wrecked it off the coast of Sumatra. Divers and companies have searched the shallow seas there for decades. Several have claimed to find it. None has proved it.

sec.h: Eggs, crowns and a scrap dealer
sec.t:
Between 1885 and 1916, the jeweller Peter Carl Fabergé made 50 jewelled eggs for the Russian royal family, each with a surprise hidden inside. After the Russian Revolution in 1917, many were sold or lost. In 2012, an American scrap dealer who had bought a little gold egg at a market searched the web and realised it was the missing Third Imperial Egg. He had nearly melted it down.

Royal treasure is still going missing today. On 19 October 2025, thieves broke into the Louvre, the world's most visited museum, and took eight pieces of jewellery that once belonged to French queens and empresses. It took them less than eight minutes. They also dropped a crown, which was found outside, broken. By mid-2026, the eight stolen pieces were still missing.

Wars, revolutions and storms are the great hiders of treasure. Objects get broken up, melted or quietly sold. Records burn. And a hunter needs luck as much as maps and [[@metal-detectors|metal detectors]]. Some of the best finds came from people who weren't looking at all. The most famous lost diamond in the story, though, isn't lost: it sits in a crown in the Tower of London, and four countries say it belongs to them.

text: Daily life in Japan mixes old customs with very modern technology. A child might take a [[@bullet-trains|high-speed train]] to visit grandparents, then take off their shoes at the door of a house with paper sliding screens. People [[@life-greetings|bow to greet each other]], say thank you before and after meals, and keep public places tidy.

About 12.4 crore people live in Japan, a chain of islands in the Pacific. Most live in crowded cities on the coast, because much of the land is steep mountains. Sharing small spaces has shaped many habits, from quiet trains to careful sorting of rubbish.

Parents who volunteer each day

st.reveal: Lunch is usually eaten in the classroom. Each day a group of students puts on white coats and caps, collects the food from the kitchen and serves their classmates. Everyone eats together, often with their teacher.

d.try: Write a haiku. A traditional Japanese haiku has three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables, and often mentions a season. Try one about something you saw today, counting the syllables on your fingers. The pattern is five, then seven, then five.
myth: People in Japan eat sushi every day.
Sushi is popular, but many families save it for treats and special occasions. Everyday meals are more likely to be rice, miso soup, grilled fish, noodles or curry rice.

sec.t:
Almost every Japanese home has a genkan, a small entrance area slightly lower than the rest of the house. You take off your outdoor shoes there and step up into the house in socks or slippers. Many schools, temples and even some restaurants do the same.

Some rooms have floors of tatami, thick mats of woven straw. Rooms are often measured by how many tatami mats fit, rather than in square metres. In many homes, people sleep on futons, thick mattresses that are folded away in a cupboard during the day.

Japanese children often walk to school in small groups, even from age six, wearing yellow hats so drivers can see them. Many carry a sturdy leather backpack called a randoseru. At school, students take turns serving lunch and clean their own classrooms each day, a habit called o-soji.

Children learn three writing systems: hiragana and katakana, which stand for sounds, and kanji, characters that came from [[@china-today|China]]. By the end of school, students learn about 2,000 kanji. Many also learn [[@origami-maths|origami]], folding paper into cranes and other shapes.

Before eating, people say "itadakimasu", roughly "I humbly receive". Meals are eaten with [[@food-chopsticks|chopsticks]], and a typical home meal might be rice, miso soup, fish and pickled vegetables. Parents often pack a bento, a lunch box with small portions neatly arranged.

Curry rice, or kare raisu, is a family favourite. It came to Japan in the late 1800s through the British, who had learned about curry in India, and the Japanese navy made it a regular meal. Japanese curry is thick, mild and slightly sweet.

sec.h: Hot baths and an ageing country
sec.t:
Japanese people love a deep hot bath, called ofuro. You wash and rinse yourself outside the tub first, then soak in clean hot water. Japan's volcanoes heat thousands of natural [[@geysers-hot-springs|hot springs]], called onsen.

Japan has one of the longest life expectancies in the world. Almost three in ten people are aged 65 or over, the highest share of any large country. This brings challenges for [[@ageing|ageing]] families and for finding enough workers, and it is one reason Japan builds [[@robots|robots]] to help care for older people.

text: New Zealand is an island country in the south-western Pacific Ocean. It has two main islands, the North Island and the South Island, and hundreds of smaller ones. In Māori, the language of its first people, it is called Aotearoa, often translated as "land of the long white cloud".

It is a land of contrasts packed close together: volcanoes and geysers in the north, [[glacier|glaciers]], fjords and the snowy Southern Alps in the south, and beaches everywhere in between. About 53 lakh people live there, and more than four times as many sheep (2024 figures). New Zealand is also famous for its strange birds, its rugby team and the films of [[@tolkien|*The Lord of the Rings*]], which were shot among its mountains.

sec.t:
New Zealand broke away from the old [[@pangaea|supercontinent]] of Gondwana about 80 million years ago, before most [[mammal|mammals]] had spread around the world. Apart from a few bats, no land mammals reached it. Birds filled their roles instead.

There were [[@lost-moa|moa]], giant flightless birds, the biggest taller than a man with its neck stretched up. The Haast's eagle, the largest eagle known, hunted them. Today the [[@penguin-flight|kiwi]], the country's national bird, is a shy, flightless night bird that sniffs for worms with nostrils at the tip of its beak. It lays one of the biggest eggs for its size of any bird.

The kākāpō is the only flightless parrot in the world, a heavy, green, owl-faced bird that waddles and climbs. Rats, cats and stoats brought by people nearly wiped it out. After decades of rescue work on predator-free islands, there are still fewer than 300. Unlike the [[@dodo|dodo]], it was saved in time, just.

{{story:dodo}}

The first people arrived about 1250 to 1300 CE. They sailed thousands of kilometres from eastern Polynesia in large double-hulled canoes, steering by stars, waves and the flight of birds. Their [[descendant|descendants]] are the Māori. Within a couple of centuries, the moa had been hunted to extinction.

In 1840, many Māori chiefs and the British Crown signed the Treaty of Waitangi. The English and Māori versions differ in important ways, especially about who would hold power and land, and arguments over it continue today. Māori language and culture, including the haka, a powerful group dance, are now part of national life. Te reo Māori became an official language in 1987.

New Zealand sits where two of Earth's plates grind together, so it has earthquakes and active [[@volcano|volcanoes]]. Around Rotorua, the ground steams and bubbles, mud pools plop and [[@geysers-hot-springs|geysers]] shoot boiling water into the air. Many homes and hotels use the underground heat.

In the South Island, the Southern Alps rise to Aoraki / Mount Cook, 3,724 metres high. Glaciers slide down the valleys, and in the south-west, Milford Sound is a fjord with walls rising straight out of dark water, just like the [[@norway-fjords|fjords of Norway]].

In 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give all adult women the [[@womens-vote|right to vote]] in national elections, after a campaign led by Kate Sheppard. Her face is on the ten-dollar note.

On the five-dollar note is [[@mountaineering|Sir Edmund Hillary]], a beekeeper from Auckland. In 1953, he and Tenzing Norgay, a [[@people-sherpas|Sherpa climber]] from Nepal and India, became the first people known to reach the top of Mount Everest. Hillary spent much of his later life building schools and hospitals for Sherpa communities in Nepal.

text: Spain is a large country in south-western Europe that covers most of the Iberian Peninsula. It has hot, dry plains in the middle, snowy mountains in the north and south, and long coasts on the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Madrid, the capital, is almost exactly in the centre.

Spain is known for its sunshine and beaches, its football clubs, its late dinners, flamenco, tapas and festivals. It is also known for its history. Muslim rulers governed much of it for centuries, and later Spanish ships built an [[empire|empire]] across the Americas. That is why [[@spanish-language|Spanish]] is now the first language of nearly 50 crore people, more than any other language except Mandarin Chinese.

st.prompt: In 1492, two famous things happened in Spain. Granada surrendered to the Spanish king and queen, ending Moorish rule. What was the other?

options.t: Columbus set sail across the Atlantic
Spain won its first football match
The first tomato arrived from America

st.reveal: In January 1492, Granada surrendered to Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand. A few months later, they paid for Christopher Columbus to sail west, hoping to reach Asia. Tomatoes came later, after Spanish explorers reached Mexico.

myth: Everyone in Spain takes a long nap every afternoon.

The siesta is a real tradition, especially in hot southern areas in summer, but surveys suggest only a minority of Spaniards nap regularly. Most people in cities work through the afternoon like people anywhere else.

sec.t:
In 711, armies from North Africa crossed the narrow strait from what is now Morocco. Within a few years they ruled most of the [[peninsula|peninsula]]. The Arabs and Berbers called it al-Andalus, a name that lives on in the southern region of Andalusia.

For hundreds of years, cities like Córdoba were centres of learning, where Muslim, Jewish and Christian scholars translated Greek books and studied medicine and astronomy. Christian kingdoms in the north slowly pushed south. The last Muslim kingdom, Granada, surrendered in January 1492.

Granada's hilltop palace, the [[@alhambra|Alhambra]], survives, with courtyards of fountains and walls carved like lace. Spanish still has thousands of words that came from [[@arabic-script|Arabic]], from *aceite* (oil) to *azúcar* (sugar), a reminder of how [[@words-borrowed|words travel]] with people.

On the last Wednesday of August, the town of Buñol near Valencia holds La Tomatina. Trucks tip over 100 tonnes of overripe tomatoes into the streets, and for one hour about 20,000 people throw them at each other. Afterwards, fire hoses wash the town clean. The festival started in 1945, reportedly with a scuffle at a parade.

Tomatoes are usually eaten, of course, in dishes like gazpacho, a cold soup, and pa amb tomàquet, bread rubbed with tomato and olive oil. Spain produces more olive oil than any other country, often close to half the world's supply.

Spaniards often eat lunch at 2 or 3 in the afternoon and dinner at 9 or 10 at night. One reason may be the clock. Geographically, Spain lines up with Britain and Portugal. But in 1940, the dictator Francisco Franco moved Spain's clocks forward one hour to match Germany and much of Europe. They never moved back, so the sun rises and sets late by the clock. Spain's [[@time-zones|time zone]] is still debated today.

In Andalusia, flamenco blends Romani, Andalusian and other traditions into fierce singing, guitar and stamping dance. UNESCO lists it as part of the world's intangible cultural heritage. And on the far side of the country, in Barcelona, the giant church of the Sagrada Família, begun in 1882 and shaped by the architect Antoni Gaudí, is still being finished.

text: Hanuman is the mighty monkey hero of the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], the ancient epic about Prince Rama. He is strong enough to lift a mountain and fast enough to leap across the sea. But what people love most is his loyalty. He never asks for anything for himself.

For Hindus, he is a god who protects, gives courage and removes fear. Truck drivers paint his face on their dashboards, wrestlers pray to him before a bout, and students recite his prayer before exams. Temples to him stand on roadsides, hilltops and street corners across India, and Tuesdays and Saturdays are special days for his worship.

st.prompt: In one well-known story, how did Hanuman get his name?

From the name of the mountain where he was born

st.reveal: In Sanskrit, "hanu" means jaw. One story says the god Indra struck the baby with his thunderbolt when he leapt at the Sun, hurting his jaw, and the name means "the one with the jaw".

In much of north India it is celebrated on the full moon of Chaitra, in spring. In Tamil Nadu it is usually marked in the month of Margazhi, in December or January, and other regions have their own dates.

sec.h: A baby who tried to eat the Sun
sec.t:
The stories start early. Hanuman's mother was Anjana and his father Kesari, and the wind god Vayu is said to be his divine father. As a hungry baby, Hanuman saw the rising Sun, thought it was a glowing fruit and jumped into the sky to grab it.

The god Indra, alarmed, struck him with a thunderbolt. Hanuman fell, hurting his jaw. In Sanskrit, *hanu* means jaw, which gives one explanation for his name. Vayu was so upset that he stopped the wind, and the world began to choke. To calm him, the gods gave the baby gifts: strength, speed and the power to change his size.

In the Ramayana, the demon king Ravana kidnaps Sita, Rama's wife, and carries her to Lanka. Hanuman makes a giant leap across the ocean to find her. He gives Sita Rama's ring as proof that help is coming.

Ravana's guards catch him and set his tail on fire. Hanuman simply grows bigger, breaks free and leaps from roof to roof, setting Lanka ablaze with his burning tail. Children have loved that part of the story for centuries.

Later, when Rama's brother Lakshmana is badly wounded, Hanuman flies to the Himalaya to fetch a healing herb called sanjeevani. Unable to tell which plant it is, he lifts the whole mountain and carries it back.

{{story:ramayana}}

What makes Hanuman different from many strong heroes is that he is humble. One famous picture shows him tearing open his chest to reveal Rama and Sita sitting in his heart. His whole strength is used in the service of others.

In the 1500s, the poet Tulsidas wrote the Hanuman Chalisa, forty verses in Awadhi, a form of Hindi. It is short enough to learn by heart, and millions of people recite it daily. It turns up in [[@devotional-music|devotional music]], films and even ringtones.

Hanuman's stories travelled with the Ramayana. In Thailand, he appears in the Ramakien as a clever, sometimes cheeky hero, and his figure decorates temple walls in Bangkok. In Indonesia, Hanuman dances in the famous kecak performance of Bali, while a circle of men chant "cak-cak-cak".

The grey langur monkeys of India are often called Hanuman langurs, and many people treat them kindly because of the stories. In many akharas, the traditional [[@wrestling-india|wrestling]] schools of north India, a Hanuman shrine stands beside the mud pit.

Hanuman is said to be a chiranjivi, one who lives forever, so many believe he still listens wherever the Ramayana is told. His friend in the temple next door is often Ganesha, the remover of obstacles, whose [[@myths-ganesha-stories|favourite stories]] include a race around the whole world.

text: Ghee is made by heating butter gently until all its water boils away. Butter is about four fifths fat, but it also holds water and a little milk [[protein|protein]]. As it simmers, the water bubbles off and the proteins sink to the bottom and turn golden brown. The cook pours off the clear, golden fat above and strains it. That is ghee.

The browned bits give ghee its nutty smell. Without its water, ghee keeps for months, and it can be heated much hotter than butter without burning. Those two things made it perfect for India's warm [[@kitchens-history|kitchens]].

st.prompt: Why can a jar of ghee stay good on a kitchen shelf for months?

options.t: It has almost no water, and most germs need water to grow
The heat leaves the ghee permanently hot inside
Ghee has salt added to it

st.reveal: Bacteria and moulds need water to live and multiply. Cooking butter into ghee drives off nearly all of it. Kept clean and covered, ghee stays fresh for a long time, though it can slowly turn stale over many months.
